files.lesson.md: --- order: 4 unit: powers node: [AC9M7N01 n1, AC9M7N01 n2] title: Squares and square roots summary: "A square number is the area of a square: 6² = 6 × 6 = 36. The square root undoes it: √36 = 6, the side of a square with area 36." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A square patio uses 49 tiles. How long is each side? Squares and square roots go back and forth between a side and an area." connection: square-pavers app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8264 url: http://127.0.0.1:8264/index.html readySelector: "#sl-s" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: square.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A square of side 6 cm covers $6 \\times 6 = 36$ unit squares: $6^2 = 36$, so $\\sqrt{36} = 6$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@square.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Side and area" say: "A square number is the area of a square." clip: - caption: { text: "Side 4: 4 rows of 4. 4² = 16.", say: "Side four: four rows of four. Four squared is sixteen." } - wait: 800 - caption: { text: "Side 5: 5 × 5 = 25, not 5 × 2.", say: "Side five: five times five is twenty-five." } - click: Make s bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "5 × 5 = 25" } - wait: 1000 - caption: { text: "Back again: √25 = 5, the side.", say: "The square root goes back: the side is five." } - wait: 1400 --- Multiply a number by itself and you get its **square**: $6 \times 6 = 36$, written $6^2$ ("6 squared"). The name comes from the shape: a square with side 6 covers 36 unit squares. Numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and 36 are **perfect squares**. The **square root** goes the other way: $\sqrt{36} = 6$, because $6 \times 6 = 36$. It is the side of a square with that area. ## Predict: 5 squared ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a value for 5² shows whether they read the small 2 as 'times 2' (10) or as 'times itself' (25)." check: type: predict q: "What is $5^2$?" options: ["25", "10", "7", "52"] actual: "25. 5² means 5 × 5: a square with side 5 has 5 rows of 5 unit squares. 10 is 5 × 2, double, not squared." ``` Picture a square with side 5. How many unit squares does it cover? ## Run: a square of 49 ```step stage: run insight: "Growing the side until the area is 49 shows the square root as the side of a square with that area." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#run", height: 540 } check: { type: board, text: "Change the side $s$ until the square's area is 49. What is $\\sqrt{49}$? Was your prediction for $5^2$ right?", when: "a = 49" } ``` $s$ is the side. The board counts the unit squares: the area. ## Investigate: squaring and its inverse ```step stage: investigate insight: "Squaring multiplies a number by itself, and the square root undoes it; Ava's mistake (5² = 10) is squaring as doubling, and its mirror is halving for a root." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\sqrt{81}$." answer: "9" feedback: - ["40.5", "That is 81 ÷ 2, half. The square root is the number that times itself makes 81."] - ["6561", "That is 81 squared. The square root goes the other way."] explain: "9 × 9 = 81, so √81 = 9." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ava" text: "Ava finds the area of a square with side 5 cm. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: square-double explain: "Line 3: 5² means 5 × 5 = 25, not 5 × 2. The area is 25 cm²." - check: type: question q: "Why is $\\sqrt{64} = 8$?" options: ["Because $8 \\times 8 = 64$", "Because $64 \\div 8 = 8$ and $64 \\div 2 = 32$", "Because 64 is even"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "64 ÷ 8 = 8 is true, but the reason is that 8 times itself makes 64.", "Many even numbers are not perfect squares, such as 50."] explain: "The square root of 64 is the number that times itself makes 64: 8 × 8 = 64." ``` ### Undo the square The square root asks: what number, times itself, makes this? ```worked 6^2 = 6 \times 6 = 36 :: Squaring: multiply the number by itself (a square with side 6). \sqrt{36} = 6 :: The square root goes back: 6 × 6 = 36, so the side is 6. 1,\ 4,\ 9,\ 16,\ 25,\ 36,\ 49,\ 64,\ 81,\ 100,\ 121,\ 144 :: The perfect squares from 1² to 12². Learn them. ``` Now try one: $\sqrt{81}$. ### Find the mistake Read Ava's working. What does the small 2 mean? ### Why it works ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: the biggest square in the list, a root, a side from an area in context, a perimeter (two steps), then a number that is not a perfect square." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#big", height: 540 } tasks: - starter: "square.yml#big" hint: "Try sides of 10, 11 and 12." check: { type: board, text: "Make a square with area 144 m².", when: "a = 144", explain: "12 × 12 = 144, so √144 = 12." } - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\sqrt{121}$." answer: "11" feedback: - ["60.5", "That is half of 121."] explain: "11 × 11 = 121." - check: type: answer q: "A square tile has area 64 cm². How long is each side, in cm?" answer: "8" feedback: - ["32", "That is half of 64. Which number times itself makes 64?"] - ["16", "16 × 16 = 256. Try a smaller side."] explain: "√64 = 8, so each side is 8 cm." - check: type: answer q: "A square garden has area 49 m². What is its perimeter, in metres?" answer: "28" feedback: - ["7", "7 m is one side. The perimeter goes all the way round: 4 sides."] - ["196", "That is 4 × 49. Find the side first: √49."] explain: "Side = √49 = 7 m. Perimeter = 4 × 7 = 28 m." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Just the side first: the garden is a square of area 49 m². How long is one side, in metres?", answer: 7, explain: "7 × 7 = 49. Now go all the way round." } - check: type: question q: "Edge case: is 50 a perfect square?" options: ["No: 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, and no whole number squares to 50", "Yes: 50 = 25 × 2", "Yes: √50 = 25"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "25 × 2 is not a number times itself.", "25 × 25 = 625, not 50."] explain: "50 is between 49 (7²) and 64 (8²), so no whole number squares to 50. The next lesson finds roots like √50." ``` ### The biggest in the list Each task changes one thing. ### A root ### A side from an area ### Two steps: the perimeter ### Not a perfect square ## Practise: squares and roots ```step stage: practise insight: "Squares, roots and a side from an area, mixed; doubling is the planted slip; the review keeps integers fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Work out $9^2$." answer: "81" feedback: - ["18", "That is 9 × 2. Squaring is 9 × 9."] explain: "9 × 9 = 81." - check: type: answer q: "Work out $\\sqrt{100}$." answer: "10" feedback: - ["50", "That is half of 100."] explain: "10 × 10 = 100." - check: type: answer q: "A square rug has area 9 m². How long is each side, in metres?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["4.5", "That is half of 9."] - ["81", "That is 9 squared. The side is the square root of the area."] explain: "√9 = 3, so each side is 3 m." - check: type: answer q: "Review: work out $-4 \\times 3$." answer: "-12" feedback: - ["12", "A negative times a positive is negative."] explain: "4 × 3 = 12, and the signs differ, so −12." ``` ### Square ### Root ### A side ### Review: integers ## Make: a bigger square ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing a perfect square past 100 and naming its root extends the list beyond 12² by the same reasoning." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["Try a side of 13 or 14.", "The area is side × side."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a perfect square bigger than 144 (past the list).", when: "a > 144", explain: "13² = 169, 14² = 196, 15² = 225: so √169 = 13, √196 = 14, √225 = 15." } ``` Then write its square root, and check by multiplying. ## Make: a square patio, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A patio laid in square pavers is a square number: the count is the area, and the side is the square root. The count is past the list, so 13 comes from testing." hint: ["The count of pavers is side × side.", "Which number times itself makes 169? Try past 12."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A square patio is laid with 169 square pavers. How many pavers are along one side?" steps: - ["The patio is a square of pavers, so $\\text{side} \\times \\text{side} = 169$", "the count of pavers is the area, in unit squares"] - ["$\\sqrt{169}$: which number times itself makes 169?", "the square root undoes squaring"] - ["$13 \\times 13 = 169$, so the side is 13 pavers", "$12^2 = 144$ is too small and $14^2 = 196$ is too big"] picks: - step: 2 q: "How do you get the side from the number of pavers?" options: - "Find the number that times itself makes 169" - "Halve 169" - "Divide 169 by 4, one for each side" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Half of 169 does not multiply by itself to make 169.", "Dividing by 4 is for a perimeter. The count is the whole area."] answer: "13" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["84.5", "That is half of 169. Which number times itself makes 169?"] - ["42.25", "That divides by 4. The count is side × side, so take a square root."] criteria: - "I wrote the count as side × side." - "I checked my side by multiplying it by itself." - "I used 12² = 144 to know the side was past 12." explain: "side × side = 169, and 13 × 13 = 169, so each side is 13 pavers." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The patio is made up for the task, and a real one has cut pavers at the edges. Write the count as side × side, find the root, check it, and type the side. **Also used in** - **Building.** Pavers, tiles and turf are bought by the count or the area, and a square layout is a square number. - **Gardens.** A square vegetable patch of 50 m² has a side of √50, between 7 and 8 m. Roots that are not whole come next. ```teacher summary: Students grow a square on a grid to see a square number as an area, learn the perfect squares to 144, and use the square root as the inverse, the side of a square with a given area (AC9M7N01, nodes 1 and 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can work out the square of a number and list the perfect squares to 144. - I can find the square root of a perfect square and explain what it means. - I can find the side and the perimeter of a square from its area. struggle: Telling squaring from doubling under time pressure. Ask students to draw the square for 5² before they answer, rather than correcting the 10. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need times tables and area as side × side (Year 6). The one idea: squaring is a number times itself (the area of a square), and the square root goes back (the side). The common mistakes are squaring as doubling (5² = 10) and rooting as halving (√36 = 18); both are planted. Recall of the perfect squares to 144 is the hinge for the next lesson (roots between whole numbers). running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 10 doubled." - "Run: ask how the board knew the area. Count one row, then the rows." - "Investigate: write 6² = 36 and √36 = 6 on the board as a pair that undo each other." - "Modify: before the perimeter task, ask what the 49 is: an area or a length?" - "Make: collect squares past 144 and their roots; look at the last digits." - "Paper: the patio task in Make is worked in books; the page marks the answer (13) and the reason for taking a root. Books out, then look for the check 13 x 13 on the page." stuck: - see: A student writes 5² = 10 (Ava's mistake). ask: Draw a square with side 5. How many unit squares? fix: "Squared means times itself: 5 × 5." - see: A student halves for a root (√36 = 18). ask: Does 18 × 18 make 36? fix: The root times itself must give the number back. - see: A student gives the side when the question asks for a perimeter. ask: How many sides go round the garden? fix: Find the side with the root, then multiply by 4. stretch: The last digits of square numbers are 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Use this to show that 2023 and 1458 cannot be perfect squares. support: Keep the list of squares to 144 visible, and use the grid board for every root. leads: > Next: Between the squares (nodes 3 and 4), then exponent notation (AC9M7N02). Where it leads: Pythagoras (Year 8) uses squares and roots on every side of a right-angled triangle. exit: q: A square has area 81 cm². Find its side and its perimeter. a: Side √81 = 9 cm; perimeter 4 × 9 = 36 cm. explain: > A **square number** is a number times itself: $6^2 = 6 \times 6 = 36$. It is the area of a square with side 6. The perfect squares to 144 are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144. The **square root** undoes squaring: $\sqrt{36} = 6$ because $6 \times 6 = 36$. It is the side of a square with area 36. (Squared is not doubled: $5^2 = 25$, not 10.) ```

# region: ava
A square has side 5 cm. Find its area.
Area = side squared.
5² = 5 × 2 = 10
So the area is 10 cm².
